q.intro.text: Eleven students timed their trip to school. Most take eight to twenty-nine minutes. One lives far out of town and takes fifty-nine minutes. Which number best describes a typical commute? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps on the same eleven commutes. Press each one. The plot moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Eleven values, already in order on the axis. Count in from both ends. The sixth dot is the middle. The median is nineteen minutes, with five commutes below it and five above.

e.step1.text: Leave the median out, and take the middle of each half. The lower five give Q one, thirteen. The upper five give Q three, twenty-six. The box runs from Q one to Q three. The I Q R is thirteen minutes, the spread of the middle half.

e.step2.text: The fence sits one and a half I Q Rs beyond the box. Twenty-six plus nineteen and a half is forty-five and a half. Fifty-nine lies beyond it, so it is an outlier. The whisker stops at twenty-nine, and fifty-nine gets its own point. The low fence, below zero, is below every commute.

e.step3.text: The mean, twenty-two, sits to the right of the median. The fifty-nine drags it up. The median and I Q R come from the middle of the ordered list, and barely notice it. Report the median, nineteen minutes, and the I Q R, thirteen minutes, for eleven students.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why report the median and I Q R here?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. With a long tail or an outlier, the median and I Q R describe the typical student better.

e.why.always.text: Not always. For a symmetric shape the mean works well, and when the total matters, you need the mean.

e.why.error.text: It is a real commute. One student lives far away. We keep it. We just choose summaries it cannot drag around.

t.intro.text: Eleven phones ran until their batteries died. One phone, with a worn-out battery, lasted only four hours. The first two steps are done for you.

t.iqr.text: What is the I Q R?

t.iqr.range.text: Twenty-three is the range, twenty-seven minus four. The I Q R is the width of the box, Q three minus Q one.

t.iqr.count.text: Seven counts the phones from eighteen to twenty-four. The I Q R is a distance on the axis, Q three minus Q one.

t.iqr.no.text: The I Q R is the width of the box. Q three minus Q one.

t.iqr.ok.text: Yes. Twenty-four minus eighteen is six hours, the spread of the middle half.

t.fences.text: Now the fences. One and a half I Q Rs below Q one, and above Q three.

t.f.noOne.text: That steps one I Q R away. The rule steps one and a half I Q Rs, which is nine, below Q one and above Q three.

t.f.ends.text: The fences start from the quartiles, not from the smallest and largest values.

t.f.no.text: One and a half times six is nine. Go nine below Q one, and nine above Q three.

t.f.ok.text: Yes. Eighteen minus nine is nine, and twenty-four plus nine is thirty-three. And four is below nine, so it is an outlier.

t.whisker.text: In the modified box plot, where does the lower whisker end?

t.w.ok.text: Yes. The whisker stops at the last real value inside the fence, and four is drawn as its own point.

t.w.fence.text: The fence is a cutoff, not a data value. No phone lasted nine hours. The whisker ends at a real value.

t.w.min.text: Four is an outlier. It gets its own point, and the whisker stops before it.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked nineteen, the median, and you were right. The long commute could not drag it.

q.cb.mean.text: At the start you picked twenty-two, the mean. One long commute dragged it up. The median, nineteen, was the typical one.

q.cb.mid.text: At the start you picked thirty-three and a half, halfway between the shortest and longest. That uses only the two extremes, and no student was near it.

q.cb.none.text: With an outlier or a long tail, report the median and I Q R. They come from the middle of the ordered data.

p.intro.text: A thermometer read five degrees too low all week. The eight daily highs had a mean of sixty-five degrees and an S D of two degrees. Sam says: every reading goes up five degrees, so the S D goes up five degrees too, from two to seven. Is Sam right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.no.larger.text: Spread is how far the values sit from each other, not how big they are. Sliding the plot keeps every gap.

p.no.observed.text: The S D is a typical distance, not a data value. Distances do not move when the plot slides.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.c1.text: Right. Watch the after plot slide five degrees. Its balance point slides with it.

p.c2.text: Right. The distance segments in both plots match, one for one.

p.c3.text: Right. Same distances, same S D. Still two degrees.

p.done.text: That's a proof. Three claims, each with its reason. Adding the same amount to every value moves the center and keeps the spread.
